summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies, including EO 14168 on binary sex classification in identity documents and federal facilities, EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding, and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last of which is paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and any marker that does not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents, while passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The American Civil Liberties Union has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, with some stranded abroad.

Partner recognition is unsettled in practice. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it. In 2015 the territory's attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still being reviewed and that he did not know, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it; no licence applications had been made. In January 2016 the Senate confirmed Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, who told a confirmation hearing he had not read Obergefell, that the district court does not deal with the ruling, and that he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws change.

A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa, one with American Samoa Legal Aid, concludes that Obergefell does apply in the territory despite those official statements and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that no same-sex couple has applied for a licence to date and sets out a litigation route through the High Court of American Samoa, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, and then the US Department of the Interior. Against that, a July 2024 on-island survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, reported by Samoa News, treats the local ban as operative and its durability under the Fourteenth Amendment as an open question, more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act of 13 December 2022 obliged recognition of marriages performed elsewhere.

Trans-specific litigation and violence are documented. In September 2023 the US Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee; in June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity; in February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Local conditions differ from the federal legal layer. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, is described in a University of Hawaii research guide as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association on an explicit cultural-pride footing. Reporting from 2009 describes homosexuality as a widely accepted part of Samoan culture while noting that reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations under the fa'amatai chiefly system.
tangentialFactors:
American Samoa's position on the federal marriage ruling was an outlier among United States territories: Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply Obergefell in 2015 while American Samoa's attorney general said applicability was still under review. The territory's Senate had already declined a statutory ban in 2003, so the divergence runs through both the legislature and the executive.

Contemporaneous testimony from a fa'afafine resident, Tifanny Poutasi, at the 2003 committee hearing stated that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek marriage with other men, citing Christian upbringing. That position is a cultural and religious one rather than a legal constraint, and it sits alongside a 2026 legal analysis reaching the opposite conclusion about what the territory is obliged to do.

Practical guidance for trans travellers and residents is carried by national organisations rather than territory-specific sources: Lambda Legal maintains an FAQ on passport and identity-document rules, name and gender change interactions with federal records and the current status of document updates, and the Human Rights Campaign publishes updated passport-rights guidance covering the elimination of the X marker and the federal court challenges to the policy.

Comparative reporting has repeatedly framed American Samoa against Fiji, where homophobic violence is described as widespread, and against the wider Samoan cultural sphere in which fa'afafine are publicly visible. The territory's small size, roughly 57,000 residents across seven islands and atolls, means trans-specific incidents are few but individually prominent in the record.
localsOnly:
Employment protection has been enforced against the territorial government itself: the September 2023 Justice Department settlement with the American Samoa Government resolved a harassment claim involving a transgender employee, and a June 2023 federal civil action alleged a hostile work environment for a transgender woman employed by the territorial government. Residents can therefore point to federal enforcement machinery rather than territory-level legislation on this point.

The Fono's March 2003 rejection of a same-sex marriage ban means there is no territorial statute prohibiting such marriages, and the Respect for Marriage Act of December 2022 requires recognition of marriages lawfully performed elsewhere. The 2026 legal analysis holds that a licence would have to be issued on application, while no couple has applied, so the practical procedure for residents remains untested.

Community organisation is centred on the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010 from the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, which frames fa'afafine identity as cultural pride rather than a departure from Samoan tradition. Public conduct is nonetheless governed by local expectations of reserved behaviour under the fa'amatai chiefly system, which applies to residents regardless of orientation.

Federal document rules apply to residents holding United States passports on the same terms as elsewhere in the country: sex assigned at birth only, M or F only, existing X-marker passports valid to expiry. Territory-level identification documents are not addressed by any source in the inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Obergefell is operative in American Samoa is unresolved in the sources. The 2026 law review article says it applies and that a certificate must be issued; the 2016 judicial confirmation exchange and the July 2024 reporting treat the local ban as the working premise. No source records a court in the territory ruling on the question, and no same-sex licence application has been made, so the conflict is not settled by practice.

No source in the inventory addresses hate-crime statutes covering gender identity in American Samoa, nor any territory-level anti-discrimination ordinance. The documented protections arise from federal enforcement actions, and their scope beyond employment is not sourced here.

Access to gender-affirming care within the territory, and the effect of EO 14168 and EO 14187 on locally funded or federally funded clinics in American Samoa specifically, is not sourced. The orders are recorded as reaching the territory through federal agencies, but no territory-level implementation detail is available.

Entry screening practice for trans travellers at the territory's port of entry, treatment of foreign visitors whose documents do not match their presentation, and any territory-specific facility or bathroom rules are not covered by any source listed. The SWS25 visa restriction attached to EO 14201 is recorded as a State Department measure, but no source states how it is applied at this territory's border.
